The standard codec (compression/decompression) algorithm for pulse code modulation (PCM) from the Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunications Union (ITU-T). A-Law is the type of PCM used in most parts of the world. The other type, mu-Law, is used in the United States and Japan.

A switch with one input and two outputs (A and B), used to send signals to any of the two output devices. For example, it can be used to select and send signal to either of two printers, A or B attached to a computer; or in telephony, to use a wireless phone to switch from A to B frequency bands. Sometimes, an A/B switch can be used in reverse order, to select between two inputs to feed one output. Abacus.

The reciprocal of the dispersive power of a substance, which is a measure of light dispersion in an optical medium. It is used to classify optically transparent materials. It is given by a function of the refractive index of a material at the Fraunhofer spectral lines f (486.1nm), d (587.6nm) and c (656.3nm) wavelengths. Its symbol is V and expressed as $$V = \frac{n_d - 1}{n_f - n_c}$$ , where $n_d$ , $n_f$ and $n_c$ are the refractive indices for the Fraunhofer spectral lines d (587.6 nm), f (486.1 nm) and c (656.3 nm). A material with a high Abbe number produces less chromatic aberration than one with a low number. Abbe numbers are used to classify optically transparent materials. For example, values of Abbe range from around 20 for very dense flint glass, around 30 for polycarbonate plastics and up to 58 for crown glass. Abbe prism.

A conjecture that is, in number theory, stated in terms of three positive integers, a , b and c , which have no common factor and satisfy $a + b = c$ . If d denotes the product of the distinct prime factors of abc , the conjecture essentially states that d cannot be much smaller than c . It was proposed in 1985 by Joseph Oesterle of the University of Paris and David Masser of the Mathematics Institute of the University of Basel in Switzerland. It is now considered one of the most important unsolved problems in number theory.

A group in which the binary operation is commutative, that is, the result of applying the group operation to two group elements does not depend on their order. It was named after a Norwegian mathematician called Niels Henrik Abel (1802 - 1829). Therefore, $ab = ba$ or $a + b = b + a$ , for all elements a and b in the group. Abelian groups generalise the arithmetic of addition of integers.

Persons or individuals may therefore, have type A, type B, type O or type AB blood group. Austrian immunologist, Karl Landsteiner first identified the A, B and O blood groups in 1901. The increase in the entropy of a substance as it moves from a perfectly ordered crystalline form at^-273 o C (0 K), where its entropy is zero, to the temperature in question. Entropy is a measure of the energy in a system that is unavailable for work. Absolute entropy values are different at different temperatures and all compounds have an absolute entropy level that is an indication of the level of randomness of the molecules. For example, at 20 °C (293K), liquid water has an absolute entropy level of 70 J mol^-1 K^-1 and water in the vapour phase has an absolute entropy value of 189 J mol^-1 K^-1 .

In statistics, absolute frequency is the number of times an event occurs. For example, if a coin is tossed twice and two heads are observed, the absolute frequency of heads is one and the relative frequency is 1/4.

In other words, it is the ratio of the mass and weight (mass/weight) of a body in vacuum or allowance must be made for buoyancy. 2. The weight of a specific number of seeds used in determining the average weight of a single seed.

The lowest temperature theoretically possible. It is zero on the Kelvin scale and it is equal to^-273.15°C. At or near this temperature molecules are theoretically motionless and the physical properties of some materials change considerably. For example, some metals lose their electrical resistance and become superconducting. The third law of thermodynamics shows that A absolute zero temperature cannot be reached, nonetheless in 1994, scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) achieved a temperature of 700 nK (1 nK = 10 -9 K), using optical lattice laser equipment to adiabatically cool caesium atoms; and in 2003, scientists at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) reached 450 pK (0.45 nK).

A state of a Markov chain from which the probability of exit is zero: a state that cannot be exited once entered. Expressed mathematically, state i is absorbing when P ( i , j ) = 1, hence P ( i , j ) = 0 for all j ≠ i .

1. In chemistry, it is the up-take of a gas by a solid or liquid or the up-take of a liquid by a solid. Absorption differs from adsorption in that the molecules undergoing absorption are taken up by the volume, not by the surface. 2. In physics, it is the transformation of the energy of electromagnetic radiation such as sound and streams of particles into other forms of energy when passing through a medium. For example, in passing through a medium, the energy of electromagnetic radiation is taken up by matter, notably electrons, to transform it to heat. 3. In biology, it is the movement of dissolved substances, molecules or fluid such as water, gases or mineral ions across the membrane of a cell by diffusion, osmosis and/or by active transport to different parts of the body of an organism where they are required to build complex substances for normal growth and development. For example, in animals, soluble food materials digested are absorbed into cells lining the gut and to the blood system for transport to all body organs. In plants, water and mineral ions are absorbed from the soil by the roots.

1. A quantity that characterises the absorption of light or any other type of electromagnetic radiation as it passes through the absorbing material. Its symbol is ε and it has the dimensions of 1/(concentration x length). The absorption coefficient depends on the absorbing material and also on the wavelength of light being absorbed. Its highest value occurs where the absorption is most intense. 2. The volume of a given gas measured at a standard temperature and pressure that will dissolve in a unit volume of a given liquid.

Any measure of the extent to which the intensity of a beam of light is reduced by passing through a distance of a solution having a molar concentration of a dissolved substance. It is also called molar absorptivity in the Beer's Law (Beer's law, Beer-Lambert law, Lambert-Beer law or the Beer-Lambert-Bouguer law), which relates the absorption of light to the properties of the material through which the light is travelling). It is the constant, a , in the Beer's law relation A = ebc , where A is absorbance (no units, since A = log 10 P0 / P), e is the molar absorbtivity with units of L mol^-1 cm^-1 , b is the path length of the sample, i.e., the path length of the cuvette in which the sample is contained. This measurement in centimetres c is the concentration of the compound in solution, expressed in mol L^-1 . Therefore, if all the light passes through a solution without any absorption, then absorbance is zero and percent transmittance is 100%. If all the light is absorbed, then percent transmittance is zero and absorption is infinite. The reason for stating the law with this equation is because absorbance is directly proportional to the other parameters, as long as the law is obeyed.

A positive integer that is smaller than the sum of its proper divisors. For example, 12 is an abundant number because it is smaller than the sum (16) of its proper divisors 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16.

A perceptual digital audio coding technique that reduces the amount of data needed to produce high- quality sound, developed by Dolby Laboratories. Perceptual digital audio coding takes advantage of the fact that the human ear screens out a certain amount of sound that is perceived as noise. Reducing, eliminating or masking this noise significantly reduces the amount of data that needs to be provided. Dolby Laboratories developed two other perceptual coding systems, AC^-1 and AC^-2. AC^-3 was the first coding system designed specifically for multichannel digital audio. It is the sound format for digital television (DTV), digital versatile discs (DVDs), high definition television (HDTV) and digital cable and satellite transmissions.

An interface specification that enables 3-D graphics to display quickly on personal computers. AGP is designed to convey 3-D images, for example, from Web sites or CD-ROMs much more quickly and smoothly than is possible today on any computer other than an expensive graphics workstation. It is especially useful in conjunction with gaming, three-dimensional (3D) video and sophisticated scientific/engineering graphics programs.

AHA provides twice the bandwidth of the traditional PCI bus architecture at 266 MB per second. It consists of a memory controller hub and an input/output (I/O) controller hub.

On the surface of the Earth, all objects fall in a vacuum with acceleration between 9.78 ms^-2 and 9.82 ms^-2 depending on latitude. A series of numbers and/or letters that allow access to a particular system. It may be a password, although passwords are generally used in conjunction with usernames. Access keys need not be attached to a specific user. Many users could use the same access key for a specific system or object without being identified as a specific user.
A LED (light emmiting diode) on the front of a computer and/or disk drive that illuminates to indicate that the computer or disk is engaged.
A directory that tells the computer running Microsoft DOS/Windows where to look if a command is not part of an internal command.

A white or pale yellow crystalline aromatic compound, with chemical formula C12 H10 , molar mass 154.21 gmol^-1 , density 1.222 g/ml, boiling point 279°C (552 K) and melting point 93.4 °C (367K). It is an intermediate in the production of some dyes, soaps, pigments, pharmaceuticals, insecticides, fungicides, herbicides and plant growth hormones.

A white crystalline powder, with chemical formula C4 H4 KNO4 S, molecular weight 201.24 g/mol, density 1.81 g/cm3 and A melting point 225 °C (498 K). A non-carbohydrate sweetener, it is about 200 times as sweet as sugar and composed of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, sulfur and potassium atoms. Unlike aspartame, Acetabulum Femur Pelvic girdle showing the acetabulum it retains its sweetness even when heated, making it suitable for cooking and baking. It is used in soft drinks and desserts, baked goods and preferred by those on low carbohydrate diets such as diabetic patients.

A colourless, flammable liquid organic compound with the chemical formula C2 H4 O, melting point^-123 °C, (150 K) and a boiling point of 20.8 °C (293.95 K). It is one of a group of chemicals known as the volatile organic compounds (VOCs). It is miscible in water, alcohol, acetone, gasoline, toluene, xylene, benzene, ether, paraldehyde and organic solvents. It is an intermediate product of higher plant respiration and also as an intermediate in the metabolism of alcohol and formed as a product of incomplete wood combustion in fireplaces and woodstoves, coffee roasting, burning of tobacco, vehicle exhaust fumes and coal refining and waste processing. Many individuals are exposed to acetaldehyde by breathing ambient air. It is highly reactive and a strong reducing agent which undergoes numerous condensation, addition and polymerisation reactions. Acetaldehyde can react violently with acid anhydrides, alcohols, ketones, phenols, ammonia, hydrogen cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, halogens, phosphorus, isocyanates, strong alkalis and amines. It is used mainly as an intermediate in the synthesis of other chemicals; and also in the manufacture of acetic acid, perfumes, polyester resins, basic dyes and drugs. O H3 C NH2.

A synthetic analgesic drug similar to aspirin having the chemical formula C8 H9 NO2 , molecular mass 151.163 g/mol, density 1.263 g/cm3 , melting point 169 °C and boiling point of 420 °C. It is effective for relieving pain such as headache, muscle pain and lower back pain; and also used in reducing fever. It has weak anti-inflammatory properties. An overdose can cause severe, often irreversible or even fatal, liver and kidney damage.

A colourless liquid with a sharp, pungent odour. Its molecular formula is C4 H6 O3 , boiling point 139.8 °C (412.9 K) and a melting point of^-73.1 °C (200.1 K). It is produced by carbonylation of methyl acetate. It is mainly used in converting cellulose to cellulose acetate, a coating material used in the production of plastics, photographic film and fabrics. It is also used in the production of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and as a wood preservative. It can be safely used to substitute ethanoyl (acetyl) group (CH3 CO-) into organic compounds.

It is characterised by loss of appetite, rapid weight loss and severe ketonuria and the smell of acetone in breath, milk and urine. : A colourless, volatile, extremely flammable liquid ketone having a pleasant odour with the chemical formula CH3 COCH3 , molar mass 58.08 gmol^-1 , density 0.791 gcm^-3 , A boiling point 56.5 o C (329.65 K) and melting point^-94.8 °C (178.35). A colourless liquid organic compound having a sweet pungent odour, with the chemical formula C6 H5 COCH3 , density 1.028 g/cm³ and a melting point of 19.6 °C (292.75 K). It occurs naturally in many foods such as apple, cheese, apricot, banana, beef and cauliflower. It is the simplest aromatic ketone and used, for example, as a chemical intermediate, as a precursor to useful resins and fragrances, and as a raw material for the synthesis of some pharmaceuticals.

A highly refractive colourless liquid, with a strong odour, chemical formula CH3 COCl, density 1.104 g/ml (liquid) and boiling point 52 °C (325 K). It is an acid chloride derived from acetic acid and used in preparing esters and in the manufacture of dyestuffs and pharmaceuticals.

An ion, which is red solid in appearance with the chemical formula Fe(C5 H7 O2 ) 3 or FeC5 H7 O2 - , molar mass 353.17 g/mol, density 1.348 g/cm3 which functions as a bidentate ligand in which two ligands can bind to a central atom. It is soluble in water and is a precursor to acetylacetonate (acac). It exists in two tautomeric forms which rapidly interconvert. It has a smell resembling that of chloroform (trichloromethane). It is widely used as a solvent in dry cleaning and degreasing. It is also used to extract oils from nuts and fruit, as an anaesthetic and fire extinguisher.

A white crystalline, weakly acidic substance with chemical formula C9 H8 O4 , density 1.40 g/cm³, melting point 135 °C (408 K), boiling point of 140°C (413 K) and decomposes. It was first synthesised by the German chemist Felix Hoffman in 1893. It is part of a group of medications called nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs work by blocking the production of prostaglandins, which are body chemicals that cause inflammation and contribute to the brain's perception of pain. Acetylsalicyclic acid is used to treat pain, rheumatic fever and inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and pericarditis; and also used to reduce fever. It has antiblood clotting effect by inhibiting the production of thromboxane (a substance in platelets that causes blood clotting and constriction of blood vessels). It is used in low doses and on long-term basis to help prevent heart attacks, strokes and blood clot formation in people at high risk of developing blood clots. It may also be given at low doses immediately to people who suffer heart attack to reduce the risk of another heart attack or of the death of cardiac tissue.

A term used to describe any thermodynamic process that occurs with neither a gain nor loss of energy between the system and its surroundings; or any thermodynamic process that occurs without heat entering or leaving a system. Since no heat enters nor leaves the system, heat (Q) is zero, hence the first law of thermodynamic becomes: ΔE in = -W, where ΔE in is the internal energy of the system and W is the work done. This process generally involves a fall or rise in temperature of the system. The term can be applied in several contexts as follows: (i) Electronically adiabatic is a reaction in which there is no change of electronic state or multiplicity. (ii) Vibrational adiabaticity is a reaction in which there is no change of vibrational state during the course of reaction. The term also applies to a process in which excess vibrational energy in the reactants appears as vibrational energy in the products or in which ground-state vibration in the reactants leads to ground state vibration in the products. (iii) Rotational adiabatic is a reaction in which excess rotational energy in the reactants appears as rotational energy in the products or in which ground- state rotation in the reactants leads to ground-state rotation in the products. 2. Organs or other structures that arise in unusual position of a plant. For example, an Adventitious Bud is a bud that develops from unusual parts such as the root tuber of sweet potato whiles an Adventitious Root is a root developing in an unusual position and does not develop from the radicle. An example of an adventitious root is roots growing from the stem of maize plant. Another example is the banyan (Ficus benghalensis) , where roots grow out of the branches forming, supporting pillars. Adventitious root system occurs commonly in monocots and pteridophytes, but also in many dicots, such as clover ( Trifolium ), ivy ( Hedera ), strawberry (Fragaria ) and willow ( Salix ). Adventitious roots and buds are very important when propagating plants via cuttings, layering and tissue culture. These roots often grow from leaf and/or stem cuttings and can develop with or without the assistance of growth hormones. Adventitious plant buds can be attached to a variety of root stock via grafting and in some plants, such as raspberries, apples and cabbage are a means of vegetative propagation.

It inflates automatically in an accident and prevents the passengers from being thrown forwards. A person in the moving car has a momentum. This momentum must be brought to zero when the car suddenly stops as a result of collision. Since the person's momentum must be reduced to zero in a very short time, it implies that the force on the person's body must be very high (Newton's second law of Motion: F = Δ mv /Δ t ). The air bag extends the interval of time over which the person's momentum is reduced to zero and as a result reduces the rate of change of momentum and hence, the force. 2. Any of a number of large inflatable bags comprising part of a spacecraft's landing system, enabling the craft to come to rest through a series of bounces to provide a softer, protective surface for a person to strike on in case of collision.

An engine that draws in continuous stream of air via an inlet duct in order to burn fuel. The air is compressed, mixed with fuel, ignited and expelled as the exhaust gas. Examples of such engine include the ramjet, scramjet, turbojet, turbofan and pulse-jet. Some vehicles, such as space planes, may be fitted with both air-breathing and rocket engines for efficient operation both within and beyond the atmosphere.

A condition in organisms, such as humans and mice, in which the organism's melanin pigmentation fails to develop, giving rise to characteristics such as light skin, white hair and pink eyes. Albinism results when the recessive alleles are inherited from both parents. It is caused by the absence of the enzyme tyrosinase, which is necessary for controlling melanin production. Albinism affects both sexes, since it affects autosomal chromosomes. Although albinism is rare in animals, any organism that makes melanin is susceptible. Examples of other organisms affected by albinism are dogs, elephants, deer, rats, snakes, some birds and plants. In animals albinism is mainly characterised by pink/red eyes and white colour (although white colour may not be the main deciding factor, as many animals are naturally white). A person or animal having albinism is called an albino. Some human albinos are sensitive to sun exposure and are susceptible to skin cancer.

Aldehydes are formed by oxidation of primary alcohols. Further oxidation yields carboxylic acids. Examples of aldehydes are methanol (formaldehyde) and ethanol (acetaldehyde). Ethanol is a carbonyl group single-bonded to a hydrogen and single-bonded to a methane. They are reducing agents. Some other types of organic compounds containg carbonyl groups are ketones and carboxylic acids.

In other words, it is the branch of mathematics in which symbols, usually letters of alphabets, represent numbers or quantities and express general relationship that hold for all members of a specified set, for example x + y = y + x . 2. The properties and laws of sets, which includes the set-theoretic operations of union ( ∪ ), intersection ( ∩ ) and complementation and the relations of set equality and set inclusion. It also provides systematic procedures for evaluating expressions and performing calculations, involving these operations and relations. The binary operations of set union ( ∪ ) and intersection ( ∩ ) satisfy many identities. Several of these identities or laws have the following names: (i) Commutative laws: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A; (ii) Associative laws: A ∪ (B ∪ C) = (A ∪ B) U C and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C). (iii) Distributive laws : A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). There are also some more important laws of set algebra. For example, Proposition 3 states that for any subsets A and B of a universal set ∪ , the following identities hold: idempotent laws given by (i) A ∪ A = A and (ii) A ∩ A = A. The de Morgan's laws are given by (i) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B' .

It is the inclusion of all the roots of polynomials with coefficients of a given set, when the given set is extended. An example is x 2 + 1 = 0, which has the smallest algebraic closed set with complex solution.

Examples are ampersand curve, bean curve, bicorn, bicuspid curve, bifoliate, bifolium, bitangent-rich curve, bow, bullet nose, butterfly curve, capricornoid, cardioid and Cartesian ovals. (iv) Quintic Curve , an algebraic curve of degree five. Examples include the Burnside curve, butterfly catastrophe curve and stirrup curve. (v) Sextic Curve , an algebraic curve of degree six. An equation of the form f ( x ) = 0, where f is a polynomial. It shows the equality of two expressions formulated by applying to a set of variables, the algebraic operations namely, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, raising to power and extraction of root. An example is 4 x 3 + 6 x 2 - 7 x + 4 = 0.

An expression containing a collection of numbers, variables and signs, positive or negative and arithmetic operations that must make mathematical and logical sense, for example, 5 x 3 - 3 y 2 + 2 xy . Two types exist: simple and compound. Simple algebraic expression has one term, called a monomial, for example, 3 a . Compound algebraic expression has two or more terms: the one with two terms, for example, 4 x + 3 y is a binomial; the one with three terms, for example, 2 x 2 - 3 x + 1, 3 m^-2 n + 5 z , is a trinomial; and the one with more than three terms is a multinomial. Alternatively, an algebraic expression may not contain any individual quantifiers and is expressed only in terms of variables and intended to be interpreted as being true for all members of some set; for example, x ( y + z ) = xy + xz .

An extension field of a base field with the property that every element of the extension is algebraic over the base. Let L/K be an extension of fields. L/K is said to be an algebraic extension field if every element of L is algebraic over K. If L/K is not algebraic and contains transcendental elements then it is a transcendental extension field. An algebraic extension of the rationals is an algebraic number field. For example, the field extension R/Q, that is the field of real numbers as an extension of the field of rational numbers, is transcendental, while the field extensions C/R and Q(√2)/Q are algebraic, where C is the field of complex numbers.

A function that may be expressed in a finite number of terms, of only the elementary algebraic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and root extraction, for example, f ( x ) = nx 3 + x 4 - 2 x . They are distinguished from transcendental functions, such as the exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions, which can be expressed only by an infinite series. Another way of saying this is that the function f ( x ) is algebraic if y = f ( x ) is a solution of an equation of the form p n ( x ) y n + ... + p 1 ( x ) + p 0 ( x ) = 0, where p 0 ( x ), p 1 ( x ), ..., p n ( x ) are polynomials in x . All polynomials are algebraic. A function that satisfies no such equation is transcendental. There are various types of algebraic functions. A rational function does not have any fractional powers of the variable or variables. Integral functions do not include the operation of division in any of their terms. A homogeneous function is one in which the terms are all of the same degree, i.e., the sum of the indices of the variables in each term is the same for every term. For example, u 4 + u 3 v + u 2 v 2 + uv 3 + v 4 is a rational, integral, homogeneous function of the fourth degree in u and v .

The study of geometries that come from algebra, in particular, from rings. In classical algebraic geometry, the algebra is the ring of polynomials and the geometry is the set of zeros of polynomials, called an algebraic variety . For instance, the unit circle is the set of zeros of x 2 + y 2 = 1 is an algebraic variety, as in all the conic sections.

Let f 1 , ..., f n be polynomials in F[ x 1 ,..., x n ]; { f 1 , ..., f n } are algebraically independent if and only if there is no non-zero polynomial A ∈ F[ y 1 , ..., y n ] such that A( f 1 , ..., f n ) = 0. If the polynomials do not satisfy this, they are said to be algebraically dependent and A is their annihilating polynomial. For example, { x 1 , x 2 } are algebraically independent, but { x 1 , x 2 , x 1 3 + x 2 2 } are not.

The root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, where the coefficient of the highest power is 1. The polynomial is of the form x n + a 1 x n^-1 + ... + a n = 0, where a 1 , ..., a n are integers; For example, x 1 = 2 + 3 is an algebraic integer, since A x 1 2 + 4 x 1 + 1 = 0 . The set of all algebraic integers is closed under addition and multiplication and therefore, a subring of complex numbers denoted by A.

A number that is the root of an algebraic polynomial. For example, in the expression x 2 = 2, the square root of 2 (√2) is an algebraic number because it is a solution of the equation x 2 = 2. Another source defines it as any number that is the root of a polynomial equation with coefficients drawn from a given field, in particular the rationals; in that case, √2 is an algebraic number, but π is not. A number which is not algebraic is called transcendental. The algebraic numbers form a field.
The total of a set of quantities, with regard to their signs, as + or -, according to the rules of addition in algebra. For example, the algebraic sum of^-2, 8 and^-1 is 5.

The set of solutions of a system of polynomial equations, over the real or complex numbers. In other words, it is a subset of an n -dimensional algebraic geometry, consisting of all points ( x 1 , ..., x n +1 ) satisfying a system of polynomial equations P α x 1 ,...,x n + 1 ( ) = α ∈ A . It is the main ingredients of the study of algebraic geometry.

A number or an expression which is not a precise divisor of a given number or expression. For example, x + 3 is an aliquot of x 2 + 9 and 3 is an aliquant part of 10.

Univalent groups derived from alkanes by removal of a hydrogen atom from any carbon atom -C n H2n+1 . The groups A derived by removal of a hydrogen atom from a terminal carbon atom of unbranched alkanes form a subclass of normal alkyl ( n -alkyl) groups H(CH2 ) n . The groups RCH2 , R2 CH (R ≠ H) and R3 C (R ≠ H) are primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl groups, respectively.

Compounds that contain cumulate double bonds, >C=C=C<, in which three carbon atoms are linked by two adjacent double bonds. The outer carbon atoms are each linked to two other atoms or groups by single bonds. The simplest example is 1,2-propadiene, CH2 =C=CH2 . Allenes are dienes (unsaturated hydrocarbon alkene containing two carbon-to-carbon double bonds) with typical reactions of alkenes. Under basic conditions, they often convert to alkynes. In an allene, the two double bonds lie in planes that are perpendicular to each other. Consequently, in an allene of the type R1 R2 C=C=CR3 R4 , the groups R1 and R2 lie in a plane perpendicular to the plane containing R3 and R4 . Under these circumstances, the molecule is chiral (molecule whose arrangement of atoms is such that it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image) and can show optical activity.

A phenomenon in which parts and organs of the same organism grow at different rates. In other words, it is the growth in part of an organism in relation to its whole body. An example is legs increasing in length faster than the arms. It is studied by measuring the mass and size of any organ or part of the body and expressed in relation to the total mass or size of the entire organism using the relation Y = bx ⍺ , where Y is the mass of the organ, x is the mass of the organism, ⍺ is the coefficient of the organ and b is a constant. It is important in studying relative growth rates.

An allyl and derivatives formed by substitution. The term 'allylic position' or 'allylic site' refers to the saturated carbon atom. A group, such as -OH, attached at an allylic site is sometimes described as 'allylic'. An allyl group is a substituent with the structural formula H2 C=CH-CH2 R, where R is the connection to the rest of the molecule. It is made up of a methylene (-CH2 -), attached to a vinyl group (-CH=CH2 ).

Carbanions, carbenium ions or radicals, formally derived by detachment of one hydron, hydride or hydrogen from the CH3 group of propene or derivatives thereof. An example is allyl cation (H2 C=CHCH2 + ).

In mathematics, often written a.e. or p.p. , it is the truth set of all values with the exception of sets on zero measure. For example, if f ( x ) = 1 for all real x , g ( x ) = 1 for all irrational x and 0 for all rational x , then f and g agree almost everywhere, since the rationals have measure zero.
The powers of 2, because the aliquot parts (proper divisors) of 2 n sum to 2 n^-1. The only known almost perfect numbers are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ..., which form the powers of 2.

Cells found in the islet cells (islets of Langerhans) of the pancreas which produce glucagon, which raises glucose (type of sugar) levels in the blood. One of the causes of elevated levels of glucose in the blood is diabetes, when the body is unable to produce enough insulin to control the body's blood glucose or sugar and the diabetic does not control the glucose level through medication, exercises, etc. If not treated, it can lead to long term complications such as cardiovascular disease, nerve damage, kidney damage/ failure, damage to the blood vessels of the retina which can lead to blindness, cataract, etc.

The disintegration of certain radioactive isotopes, causing the spontaneous emission of an alpha ( ) particle. An alpha particle is a stable particle formed from two protons and two neutrons and is identical to the nucleus of the helium atom. The general reaction for alpha decay is A Z X → A^-2 Z^-4 Y + 2 4 He , where X is the parent nuclide, Y is the daughter nuclide, Z is the atomic mass of X and A is the atomic number of X . The atomic number or the number of protons decreases by two and the mass number decreases by four as a result. Alpha decay commonly occurs in elements such as bismuth with atomic numbers greater than 83. It can occur in some rare-earth elements such as neodymium and lutetium with atomic numbers between 60 and 71.

The most common form of secondary structure of proteins in which the polypeptide chain is coiled into a helix. This is a right-handed coiled or spiral conformation, in which every backbone N-H group donates a hydrogen bond to the backbone C=O group of the amino acid four residues earlier. The -helix is the most regular and the most predictable from sequence, as well as the most prevalent.

A stream or rays of relatively low penetrating power alpha particles emitted by radium and other radioactive substances moving at high speed of up to one tenth of the speed of light (1/10 × 299 792 458 m/s) but having small masses. Alpha radiations or rays are the least penetrating of the three radiations (alpha, beta and gamma) and can be stopped or absorbed by a sheet of paper and can be slightly deflected by a strong magnetic or electric field. Although radiation can be harmful, it is also useful. One use of alpha radiation is in smoke detectors. For example, radioactive americium releases alpha radiation, which ionises the air inside a fire detector. Smoke from a fire absorbs alpha radiation, altering the ionisation and triggering an alarm. Alpha rays penetrate only a small distance in dense matter such as living tissue and have been used to cause local destruction of tissue such as in cancer therapy.

The scattering of alpha particles by thin films of heavy metals, notably gold, a phenomenon explained by Ernest Rutherford in 1911. The patterns produced by such scattering offan extremely thin sheet of gold were early evidence that atoms contain a tiny, positively charged core, what is now called the atomic nucleus. This led to the development of the Rutherford model(planetary model) of the atom and eventually to the Bohr model. Rutherford scattering is also sometimes referred to as Coulomb scattering because it relies only upon static electric (Coulomb) forces and the minimal distance between particles is set only by this potential. Rutherford backscattering is any technique using high energy particles directed toward a sample, in which the bombarding particles are detected and recorded as function of energy and/or angle. The technique is mostly used for determining depth distributions of elements based on the energy of the backscattered particle. In general, He + or H + particles are used at energies in the order of 100 keV to some MeV.

Alternate angles are equal if and only if the lines are parallel. For example, in the diagram, angles a and b alternate, which means a is equal to b ( a = b ), so are c and d ( c = d ).

Electric current that changes direction periodically. If a graph of the current against time is plotted it is in a wave form, with its value varying periodically around zero. AC can come in a number of forms, as long as the voltage and current are alternating. The most common type of AC is the sine wave. The AC in homes and offices have an oscillating voltage that produces a sine wave. There are three parts to a sine wave: amplitude, frequency and phase. Some other waveforms include ths square waves, often used in digital and switching electronics to test their operation; and triangle waves, found in sound synthesis and are useful for testing linear electronics like amplifiers. The frequency of alternating current (AC) is measured in hertz. Typical equations describing an AC current and AC voltage are: I = I O sin ωt = I O sin2 πft and V = V o sin ω t = V o sin2 π ft , where ωt = 2 π f and f = 1/ T , T is the period of the signal in seconds, f is the frequency in Hz, ωt is the angular velocity in radian per second, I and V are the instantaneous values of the current and voltage respectively and I O and V O are the peak current and voltage respectively. The frequency of the domestic supply is different in different parts of the world. In Europe and most parts of the world, it is 50 Hz and in the U.S., it is 60 Hz.

Any subgroup of the symmetric or permutation group on a set S consisting of all even permutations of n objects. It is denoted by A n , has order n !/2 and has index 2 in S n , the symmetric group of degree n . For n ≥ 5, A n is the only proper non-trivial normal subgroup of S n and is itself simple.

Clouds composed of flattened globules that may be arranged in groups. They are small, white, puffy clouds composed primarily of water droplets that sometimes slowly drift across the sky and forms at altitudes of between 2000 - 6000 metres above the ground with a vertical velocity of 0.05 ms^-1 to 0.1 m s^-1 . Altocumulus clouds usually form in a layer of moist air, where air currents undulate gently, like waves on the sea. As a wave rises, water vapour condenses and forms the cloud. In the wave troughs, water evaporates. There the cloud is thinner or the sky may be clear, producing the bands of cloud that are sometimes seen.

A family of inorganic compounds, with chemical formula Al 2 O3 , density 3.95-4.1 g/cm3 , melting point 2072 °C (2345 K) and boiling point 2977 °C (3250 K). It is a white powder, soluble in most alkalis or caustic, strong acids but insoluble in water. It is widely distributed in clays, slates and shale. It is used in the production of aluminium metal, as an abrasive due to its hardness and as a refractory material due to its high melting point, as well as for ceramics and electrical insulation.

A colourless or white crystalline compound with the chemical formula Al 2 (SO4 ) 3 .K2 SO4 .24H2 O, relative density 1.757, molar mass 474 g/ mol, melting point 92-93 °C (365-366 K) and boiling point 200 °C (473 K). It occurs naturally as the mineral kalinite salt and can be prepared by recrystallisation from a solution containing equimolar quantities of potassium sulfate and aluminium sulfate. It forms cubic or octahedral crystals that are soluble in cold water, very soluble in hot water but insoluble in ethanol and acetone. Its uses include as a mordant for dyeing and in the tanning and finishing of leather goods (for white leather).

Solar irradiance in space just above the atmosphere of the Earth on a plane perpendicular to the direction of the Sun. In other words, it is the spectrum outside the atmosphere. AM is the acronym for air mass , which is the optical path length through the Earth's atmosphere for light from a celestial source. Air mass normally indicates relative air mass, the path length relative to that at the zenith at sea level. The value of the air mass is often given by appending its value to AM, so that AM1 indicates an air mass of 1, AM2 indicates an air mass of 2, etc. On average the extraterrestrial irradiance is 1367 Watts/metre 2 (W/m2 ). This value varies by ±3% as the Earth orbits the Sun. The Earth's closest approach to the Sun occurs around January 4th and it is furthest from the Sun around July 5th. Solar cells used for space power applications, such as those on communications satellites are generally characterised by AM0.

A silvery, shiny radioactive metallic transuranic element belonging to the actinoids, with the chemical symbol Am and atomic number 95, melting point 1176 o C (1449 K), boiling point 2011°C (2284 K), density 12 g cm^-3 and the mass number of the most stable isotope is 243. It was discovered in 1944. It is obtained from the beta decay of plutonium and it is a source of alpha particle used in research. It is also commonly used in smoke alarms.

Two different numbers so related that the sum of the proper divisors of each is equal to the other. For example, the pair of numbers 220 and 284 are said to be amicable numbers in the sense that the sum of the proper positive divisors of each, sum to the other. For 220 ⇒ 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 10 + 11 + 20 + 22 + 44 + 55 + 110 = 284; and for 284 ⇒ 1 + 2 + 4 + 71 + 142 = 220.

A colourless, pungent smelling gas, with the chemical formula NH3 , melting point^-77.73°C (195 K) and boiling point^-33.34°C (240 K), which is lighter than air and forms a minute proportion of the atmosphere. It is very soluble in water, giving an alkaline solution. It turns moist red litmus paper blue and forms white fume with concentrated hydrochloric acid. It is found in volcanic gases and as a product of decomposition of animal and vegetable matter. It may be produced from coal or by the Haber- Bosch process. A white crystalline solid, with the chemical formula (NH4 ) 2 CO3 , density 1.50 g/cm3 , melting point 58°C (331 K), decomposes at a boiling point and readily sublimes at room temperature and breaks down slowly into its constituent gases: ammonia, carbon dioxide and water. It is manufactured by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium carbonate and recovering the product as a sublimed solid. It is used in dyeing, wool preparation and in baking powder.

A colourless, crystalline solid with the chemical formula NH4 NO3 , density 1.725 g/cm3 , melting point 169.6 °C (442.75 K), which decomposes at 210 °C (483 K) and is prepared by the neutralisation of nitric acid with ammonia. It is used in fertilisers, herbicides, insecticides and explosives.

A colourless, water-soluble crystalline compound with chemical formula NH4 SCN, density 1.305 g/cm3 , melting point 149.5 °C (423 K), which decomposes at 170 °C (443 K). It is made from ammonia and carbon sulfide in ethanol. On heating, it turns into its isomer thiourea, SC(NH2 ) 2 . Its solutions give a characteristic blood-red colour with iron (III) compounds and so are employed as a test for ferric iron. It is used as a rapid fixative in photography and as an ingredient in making explosives.

Amount of a constituent divided by the volume of the mixture. For entities B it is often denoted by [ B ]. The antiderivative of a function ƒ ( x ) is a function F ( x ) whose derivative equals ƒ ( x ). For example, the function F ( x ) = x 5 /5 is an antiderivative of f ( x ) = x 4 . Since the derivative of a constant is zero, x 4 has an infinite number of antiderivatives such as ( x 5 /5) - 10, ( x 5 /5) + 2, etc. Thus, all the antiderivatives of x 4 can be obtained by changing the value of C in F ( x ) = ( x 5 /5) + C ; where C is an arbitrary constant known as the constant of integration. Basically, the graphs of antiderivatives of a given function are vertical translations of each other, with each graph's location depending on the value of C . Antiderivatives are related to definite integrals through the fundamental theorem of calculus and they are important because they can be used to compute definite integrals.

The reverse process of differentiation or a process of solving for antiderivatives. In other words, it is the process of finding an antiderivative for a given function; especially when deriving an indefinite integral or when evaluating a definite integral using the fundamental theorem of calculus rather than as an infinite sum of infinitesimal elements. The symbol f ( x )dx ∫ indicates the operation of antidifferentiation on f ( x ), which is the function being antidifferentiated or integrated and known as integrand. This formula works because the derivative of a constant is zero. For example, x 2 is the antiderivative of 2 x , because 2 x is the derivative of x 2 .

A Greek mathematician who worked on levers and other aspects of mechanics. He formulated the Archimedes' principle and in hydrostatics, he devised a pump called the Archimedian Screw. A law of physics named after its discoverer, Archimedes of Syracuse that concerns the upward force or upthrust on any object fully or partly submerged in a fluid. It states that the buoyant force on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Mathematically, (buoyant force) Fb = m f g ... ., where m f is the mass of the fluid displaced by the body. Archimedes' principle can be expressed in other words that an object in a fluid such as water experiences an upthrust from the fluid which is equal to the weight of the fluid that the body displaces. The upward force is called the upthrust or buoyant force, expressed mathematically as: Upthrust = weight in air - weight in liquid. The resultant force on the A body is the difference between the upthrust and the body's weight. This difference is zero for a floating body, ie. upthrust and weight are equal and opposite. Hot air displaces a balloon, producing upthrust. This upthrust is balanced by the weight of the balloon. A hot air balloon rises when the upthrust on it is greater than its weight. A diver may attach lead weight to his suit if he wants to reach a greater depth. His weight will then be greater than the upthrust on him. For a given body to float in a given fluid depends on its weight and volume or the relative density (weight per unit volume). This is compared to that of the fluid in order to determine its buoyant force. If the body is less dense than the fluid, it will float. If the body is denser than the fluid, it will sink. The principle applies to both floating and submerged bodies and to all fluids, i.e., liquids and gases. Archimedes' principle is an important and underlying concept in the field of fluid mechanics.

A non-carbohydrate sweetener used in food under various trade names such as Naturasweet, Canderel and Equal. Aspartame loses its sweetness when heated and it is usually not suitable for baking. Aspartame is favoured as a sweetener by those on low carbohydrate diet such as diabetics, some athletes and actors/actresses and all other people who need to watch their weights. Drinks such as Diet Coca Cola, Coca Cola Zero, Diet Pepsi, some chewing gums such as Wrigleys Airwaves and Orbit and some other store-bought foods such as cereals contain aspartame. Some other artificial non-caloric sweeteners include saccharin, sucralose, neotame and acesulfame potassium. Some other natural product sugar substitutes include sorbitol or xylitol.

It is formed by a transamination, in which the amino group of glutamic acid is transferred to oxaloacetic acid so forming aspartic acid. Breakdown is by the reverse reaction, followed by further oxidation in the TCA cycle. Aspartate is an important precursor of nitrogenous compounds. The amino acids leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine and lysine are all derived from aspartic acid and it is necessary for synthesis of purines, pyrimidines and porphyrins. Aspartate also acts as an amino- group donor in several reactions.

A naturally occurring carboxylic acid, with the chemical formula CH3 COOC6 H4 COOH, density 1.40 g/cm³, melting point 135°C (408 K) and boiling point 140 °C (413 K) and decoposes. Aspirin is part of a group of medications called nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is commonly used in tablet form to relieve pain and reduce fever and inflammation and also as an antiplatelet agent by inhibiting the production of thromboxane. It is also used long-term, at low doses, to help prevent heart attacks, strokes and thrombosis or blood clot formation in people at high risk of developing blood clots. Low doses of aspirin may be given immediately after a heart attack to reduce the risk of another heart attack or of the death of cardiac tissue. The undesirable side-effects of aspirin taken by mouth include gastrointestinal ulcers, stomach bleeding and tinnitus, especially in higher doses.

The rest mass of an atom in its ground state or the weighted average mass of the isotopes of an element. Its symbol is m a . The commonly used unit is the unified atomic mass unit (amu). A unit used to express the mass of individual atoms. It is expressed as the mass equal to 1/12 th of the mass of a carbon^-12 isotope. It has a value of 1.6605402 (10) × 10 -27 kg. A mass expressed on this standard is called a relative atomic mass (r.a.m.), with the symbol A r . The symbol for amu is u and that for dalton is Da. One dalton is approximately equal to the mass of one proton or one neutron.

Former name for relative atomic mass , defined as weighted average of the masses of the constituent isotopes of a chemical element or the ratio of the average mass of a chemical element's atoms to 1/12 th the mass of an atom of the carbon^-12 isotope. Its symbol is Ar. Measuring the masses of atoms in grams, for example, would imply dealing with extremely small numbers, thus, the mass of an atom is compared with that of an atom of carbon^-12. In calculating the relative atomic mass of an element with isotopes, the relative mass and proportion of each is taken into account. The cations formed are brought down on to a detector in turn according to their mass-to-charge ratio. Through the use of this instrument he discovered the existence of isotopes of elements. Relative atomic masses have no units.

Ratio of the natural log of 2 to the half-value thickness of material. It is a constant used to calculate the intensity of X-rays given any thickness of material. It shows how easily a material can be penetrated by a beam of light, sound, particles, or other energy or matter. Its symbol is μ. Any living organism that synthesises organic substances from inorganic molecules by using light or chemical energy. Autotrophic nutrition or holophytic nutrition is characteristic of organisms possessing chlorophyll (eg. Cynobacteria, Euglena, Spirogyra/green algae, green plants) by trapping light and combining inorganic substances, carbon dioxide and water to produce food by photosynthesis. Autotrophs are the primary producers in all food chains since the materials they synthesise are the energy sources of all other organisms. Autotrophs produce their own sugars, lipids and amino acids using carbon dioxide as a source of carbon and ammonia or nitrates as a source of nitrogen. Organisms such as the green plants, certain algae and the pigmented sulfur bacteria that use light energy to synthesise organic compounds are called photosynthetic autotrophs . Organisms including the iron bacteria, the nitrifying bacteria and the nonpigmented sulfur bacteria that oxidise such compounds as hydrogen sulfide (H2 S) to obtain energy are called chemosynthetic autotrophs or chemotrophs . Heterotrophs are organisms that must obtain their energy from organic compounds. Autotrophic means capable of synthesising organic substances from inorganic molecules by using light or chemical energy.

A class of plant growth hormones that promote stem and root growth and development. Some of the most important auxins include: indole^-3-acetic acid, 4-chloroindole^-3- acetic acid, Indole^-3-butyric acid and 2-phenylacetic acid.

A distillation technique employed in separating azeotropic mixtures by the addition of a third compound called the entrainer, which associates with one of the compounds of the mixture to form a third azeotrope but not the other components of the original azeotrope and makes it possible to distil this new azeotrope and separate it from the original mixture. 1. In astronomy, it is the arc of the horizon or the angular distance measured clockwise between a celestial object and the northern point of the horizon as seen by the observer. In other words, it is measured from the north point of the horizon to the intersection with the horizon of the vertical circle passing through a celestial body. In navigation, it is the angular distance usually measured clockwise from the north point of the horizon to the intersection with the horizon of the vertical circle passing through a celestial body. 2. In polar coordinates, it is also known as amplitude , argument or anomaly , which is the angle between the positive real axis and the vector representing a given complex number in the Argand diagram. One of the four quantum numbers of an atomic orbital that determines its orbital angular momentum and describes the shape of the orbital. In other words, it is one of the four quantum numbers that determines the magnitude of the angular momentum of the electron around the nucleus. It also describes the shape of the orbital. It is denoted as l and takes the values 0, 1, 2, ..., n^-1, where n is the principal quantum number. Azimuthal quantum numbers 0, 1, 2 and 3, correspond to the s , p , d and f orbitals, respectively.

An organic compound containing at least one of two doubly bonded nitrogen atoms with each atom linking two other groups through single bonds: R-N=N-R', in which R and R' can be either aryl or alkyl, for example, PhN=NPh, azobenzene. The more stable derivatives contain two aryl groups. The N=N group is called an azo group . An example of an azo compound is azo dye, which is a synthetic dye containing the azo group of two nitrogen atoms (-N=N) connecting aromatic ring compounds. Azo dyes are usually red, brown or yellow and make up about half the dyes produced. They are manufactured from aromatic amines.

A chemical equation in which the total number of atoms and charges of each element on the left hand side is equal to the total number of the same atoms and charges on the right hand side. For example, the reaction between tetraoxosulfate(VI) acid (H2 SO4 ) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to form sodium tetraoxosulfate(VI) (Na 2 SO4 ) and water can be written as: NaOH + H2 SO4 → H2 O + Na 2 SO4 . This is an incomplete equation, since the same number of atoms does not appear on both sides of the reaction (for example, one sodium atom appears in the reactants, but two sodium atoms appear in the products). Such a reaction could not actually occur. Correcting this fault is called balancing the equation. Placing a 2 in front of the NaOH balances the number of sodium atoms, as well as the hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The balanced equation therefore is: 2NaOH (aq) + H2 SO4 → 2H2 O (l) + Na 2 SO4(aq) . This equation implies that two molecules of NaOH are necessary to react with each molecule of H2 SO4 . Photosynthesis can be represented by the following chemical equation: 6CO2 + 6H2 O ------> C6 H12 O6 + 6O2 .

It is the numerical difference between the upper and lower frequencies of a band of electromagnetic radiation, especially an assigned range of radio frequencies. 2. For analogue signals such as human voice it is the difference between the highest and lowest frequency components, measured in hertz (cycles per second). For example, human voice, which produces analogue sound waves, has a typical bandwidth of three kilohertz between the highest and lowest frequency sounds it can generate. 3. In data communication and computer networks, a bandwith of a communication link is the amount of bits that can be transmitted across the links in one second. It is measured in bits per second (bit/s). Also, it is the amount of information available or consumed data communication resources expressed in bits per second (bit/s), kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, etc.). For example, a modem with a B bandwidth of 56 kilobits per second (Kbps) can transmit a maximum of about 56,000 bits of digital data in one second. 4. In linear algebra, it is the width of the non-zero terms around the diagonal of a matrix.

The equilibrium constant K b for the base ionisation; or a reaction in which a weak base is in equilibrium with its conjugate acid in aqueous solution. For example, ammonia ionizes in water as follows: NH3( aq ) + H2 O ( l )  NH4 + ( aq ) + OH - ( aq ) The base-ionisation equilibrium constant is the mathematical product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products of this reaction divided by the equilibrium concentration of the original base. In other words, Kb is the product of the concentrations of the products over the concentration of the reactants (not including water). As the Kb value of a base increases, so does the strength of the base. For a strong base: K b > 1 and for a weak base: K b < 1. The value is sometimes expressed as the logarithm of its reciprocal, called pK b . Therefore pK b = -logK b . The smaller the value of pK b , the stronger the base. K b is a better measure of the strength of a base than pH because adding more water to the base solution will not change the value of the equilibrium constant K b , but it will change the H + ion concentration. Water is not included in the base-ionisation equilibrium expression because the [H2 O] has no effect on the equilibrium.

The number of chromosomes in a genome, usually between six and thirteen and is represented by the symbol x. In diploid organisms the number of chromosomes in the genome is equivalent to the haploid number n and so 2 n = 2 x . Any of a set of seven International System of Units (SI) without combination from which all units of physical quantities can be derived.The seven S.I. base units are as follows: metre with the symbol m for length, kilogram with the symbol kg for mass, second with the symbol s for time, ampere with the symbol A for electric current, kelvin with the symbol K for temperature, candela with the symbol cd for luminous intensity, and mole with the symbol mol for amount of substance. These seven units are called base units because none of them can be expressed as combinations of the other six. Some combination base units are given special names, for example, the kilogram metre per second squared (kg·m·s^-2 ) is called the newton (N) and the kilogram metre squared per second squared (kg·m2 ·s^-2 ) is called the joule (J).

In mathematics, it refers to a number, a fact or idea that can be instantly recalled without having to use any special operations to recall them. For example, in basic classes some additions (such as 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 1 + 0 = 1, etc.); subtractions (such as 1 - 1 = 0, 2 - 1 = 1, etc.); and multiplications (1 - 10 multiplication tables), etc., are memorised forever so that there is no need to use any special operations to recall them.

The equation used in probability which allows the user to calculate the probability of an event occurring provided that another event whose probability is already known has occurred. Mathematically, Bayes' theorem gives the relationship between the probabilities of A and B , P ( A ) and P ( B ) and the conditional probabilities of A given B and B given A , P ( A │ B ) and P ( B │ A ), respectively. In its most common form, it is expressed as P ( A │ B )= , the meaning of this statement depends on the interpretation of probability ascribed to the terms. Bayes' theorem was named after the Reverend Thomas Bayes (1702-61), who studied how to compute a distribution for the probability parameter of a binomial distribution. It has applications in fields such as science, engineering, medicine and law.

The absolute value of the difference in frequency of two waves. It is the fluctuation produced in musical acoustic when two notes of nearly equal pitch or frequency are heard together. Beats result from the interference between the sound waves of the notes. The beat frequency equals the difference in frequency of the notes. Given oscillations at two frequencies, f 1 and f 2 , their beat frequency is f beat = | f 1 - f 2 |, where f 1 > f 2 .

An international system of recording wind velocity, usually made at 10 metres above ground level; and indicated by numbers ranging from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane. The Beaufort number 0 means calm and wind speed of less than 1 km/h; and 12 is a hurricane with wind speed of more than 118 km/h and waves over 13 m and greatly reduced visibility. It was invented in 1806 by Admiral Sir Francis Beaufort (1774-1857), British hydrographer and a naval officer.

The SI unit for the measurement of radioactivity. Its symbol is Bq and it is named after Henri Becquerel, who shared a Nobel Prize with Pierre and Marie Curie for their work in discovering radioactivity. One Bq is defined as the activity of a radioisotope decaying at the rate of 1 nucleus disintegration per second. The Bq unit is equivalent to s^-1 .

Any of 3000 species of bees divided into 19 families in the order Hymenoptera. It is a large insect of about 2 mm^-4 cm long; solitary or social in habit and living on nectar and pollen to produce wax and honey. Some species of bees have stingers. Bees are dependent on pollen as a protein source and on flower nectar or oils as an energy source. Adult females collect pollen primarily to feed their larvae. The pollen they inevitably lose in going from flower to flower is important to plants because some pollen lands on the pistils of other flowers of the same species, resulting in cross-pollination. They are the most important pollinating insects and their interdependence with plants makes them good examples of the type of symbiosis called mutualism. Most bees have specialised branched or feathery body B hairs that help in the collection of pollen. Female bees, like many other hymenopterans, have a defensive sting. Some bees produce honey from flower nectar. Honey bees and stingless bees commonly store large quantities of honey, which is exploited by beekeepers, who harvest the honey for human consumption.

The audio signal given out by a computer to announce the result of a short diagnostic testing sequence the computer performs when first powering up (called the Power-On-Self-Test or POST). The Power-On-Self-Test is a small program contained in the computer's Basic Input/Output Operating System (BIOS) that checks to make sure necessary hardware is present and required memory is accessible. If everything tests out correctly, the computer will typically emit a single beep and continue the starting-up process. If something is wrong, the computer will display an error message on the monitor screen and announce the errors audibly with a series of beeps that vary in pitch, number and duration. This is especially useful when the error exists with the monitor or graphic components.

It states that the fraction of incident light absorbed by a solution at a given wavelength is related to the thickness of the absorbing layer and the concentration of the absorbing substance. The law is accurate only for dilute solutions; deviations from the law occur in concentrated solutions because of interactions between molecules of the solute, the substance dissolved in the solvent.

An experiment in which there are two possible independent outcomes, named after Swiss mathematician and physicist, Jacob Bernoulli (1654-1705). It usually denotes success and failure, with the properties that the probability of occurrence of each outcome is the same in each trial and the occurrence of one excludes the occurrence of the other in any given trial. For example, in tossing a coin, the outcome has only two possibilities: either the coin lands head or tail. Let p be the probability of success in a Bernoulli trial and q , the probability of a failure, then the probability of failure, q is given by: q = 1 - p . Random variables describing Bernoulli trials are often encoded using the convention that 1 = "success", 0 = "failure". Therefore, the probability distribution of such a random variable (termed a Bernoulli distribution) is given by P ( x = r ) = nCrPrqn- r .

The spontaneous emission of beta particle from a nucleus. Beta decay is accompanied by neutrino emission and a release of energy. It is any of three processes of radioactive decay: electron emission, positron emission and electron capture in which a nucleus emits an electron or beta particle. With this sort of decay the electrons or beta particles are known as beta radiation. Beta decay is a slower process than gamma or alpha decay, but capable of penetrating hundreds of times farther than alpha particles. There are two types of beta decay where the beta particle is either an electron, called beta-minus (β - ) decay or a positron called beta-plus (β + ) decay. In beta-plus decay, a proton in an atomic nucleus decays into a neutron, a positron and a neutrino. The positron and neutrino are emitted from the nucleus, while the neutron remains by the reaction: where X is the parent atom, Y is the daughter atom, Z is the atomic mass of X , A is the atomic number of X . The electron and antineutrino are emitted from the nucleus, while the proton remains. The atomic number of the atom is thereby increased by 1. An example of beta-minus decay is the decay of Carbon^-14 into Nitrogen^-14, used in carbon dating.

In inorganic chemistry, it is an intermediate form in the deprotonation of carbonic acid. Many bicarbonates are soluble in water at standard temperature and pressure. Bicarbonate is alkaline and it is a vital component of the pH buffering system of the human body. The most common salt of the bicarbonate ion is sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3 , which is used as baking powder. The flow of bicarbonate ions from rocks weathered by the carbonic acid in rainwater is an important part of the carbon cycle.

A hypothetical explosive event that marked the origin of the universe as we know it. It refers to the idea that the universe is believed to have emerged from a single point approximately 13.7 billion years ago and was originally extremely hot and dense and has since cooled by expanding to the present diluted state and continues to expand today. The following evidence supports the Big Bang Theory: observation of the expansion of the universe, the existence and near uniformity of the cosmic microwave background radiation and the relative proportion of the element in the early universe as observed in young galaxies. In order to recreate the conditions immediately after the big bang, a 5 billion dollar instrument called the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) was designed and installed near the Swiss-French border. In 2008, two beams of protons were fired into a 27 kilometre long tunnel which houses the LHC, with the first beam moving clockwise and the second moving anticlockwise together with cataclysmic force and they are expected to collide. The beams successfully completed their lapse contrary to the fear that it might create a black-hole which will end the world. According to the best available measurements as of 2010, the initial conditions occurred around 13.3 to 13.9 billion years ago.

The concentration of glucose in the blood, normally expressed in millimoles per litre (mmol/l). The normal range is 3.5 - 5.5 mmol/l. Blood-sugar is an important investigation in a variety of diseases, most notably in diabetes mellitus.

A model of the atom conceived by Neil Bohr (1885-1962) in 1913 based on his observations of the atomic emissions spectrum of the hydrogen atom. The model assumes the following: (i) that the electrons revolve in orbits of specific radius around the nucleus without emitting or absorbing radiation; (ii) that within each orbit, an electron has a fixed amount of energy; and (iii) that emission or absorption of energy (photons) occurs between transitions. The energy absorbed or emitted can be calculated using the relation E2 - E1 = hf = h c λ , where E is the energy level, h is the Planck's constant (6.63 x 10 -34 Js, f is the frequency of the emitted photon, c is the speed of light (3.0 x 10 8 m/s) and λ is the wavelength.

A theory published in 1913 by Neils Bohr (1885-1962), a Danish physicist, which explains the line spectrum of hydrogen. It assumed that a single electron of mass m travelled in a circular orbit of radius r , at a velocity v , around a positively charged nucleus. The angular momentum of the electron would then be mvr . Bohr proposed that electrons could only occupy orbits in which this angular momentum had certain fixed values, h /2 π , 2 h /2 π , 3 h /2 π , ..., nh /2 π , where h is the Planck constant. This means that the angular momentum is quantized, i.e. it can only have certain values, each of which is a multiple of n . Each permitted value of n is associated with an orbit of different radius and Bohr assumed that when the atom emitted or absorbed radiation of frequency ν , the electron jumped from one orbit to another, with the energy emitted or absorbed by each jump being equal to hν . This theory gave good results in predicting the lines observed in the spectrum of hydrogen and simple ions such as He + , Li 2+ , etc. The idea of quantized values of angular momentum was later explained by the wave nature of the electron. Each orbit has a whole number of wavelengths around it; i.e. nλ = 2 πr , where λ is the wavelength and n a whole number. The wavelength of a particle is given by h / mv , so nh / mv = 2 πr , which leads to mvr = nh /2 π . Modern atomic theory does not allow subatomic particles to be treated in the same way as large objects and Bohr's reasoning is somewhat discredited. However, the idea of quantized angular momentum has been retained.

A radioactive transactinide element, with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is the heaviest member of Group VIIB first made in 1981 by Peter Armbruster and a team in Darmstadt, Germany, by bombarding bismuth^-209 nuclei with chromium^-54 nuclei. Its most stable known isotope, 270 Bh, has a half-life of 61 seconds. Chemical experiments have confirmed bohrium's predicted position as a heavier homologue to rhenium with the formation of a stable +7 oxidation state. Only a few atoms of bohrium have ever been detected.

The physical constant relating energy at the particle level with temperature observed at the bulk level, with the symbol k or k B . It is given by the universal gas constant divided by the Avogadro's constant, k = R/N A . It may be thought of, therefore, as the gas constant per molecule. It was named after Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906), an Austrian physicist.

An equation concerning the entropy S of a system derived from statistical mechanics. The formula is S = k ln W , where k is the Boltzmann constant and W is the number of distinguishable ways of describing the system. It expresses in quantitative terms the concept that entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system.

A strong force of attraction holding atoms together in a molecule or crystal. In other words, it is the electrostatic force of attraction between two chemical species (ions, atoms, molecules). The various types include the following: (i) ionic or electrovalent bond that is created during the formation of a compound by transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another, the resulting oppositely charged ions being held together by attraction; (ii) covalent bond , in which the attractive force between atoms is created by the sharing of electrons; and (iii) metallic bond , which is the electrostatic force between delocalised electrons and positively charged metal ions characteristic of metals. The electrons are shared between atoms and move about in the crystal. Typically chemical bonds have energies of about 1000 kJ mol^-1 .

The main component of the skeletal system or the hard connective tissue that makes up the skeleton of a vertebrate. It is one of the hardest animal tissues found in only vertebrates. It consists of collagen, a protein which gives it its tensile strength and calcium phosphate which gives it its hardness. Bones perform a variety of functions, including structural and mechanical; protecting vital organs; providing a site for the production of blood cells; and serving as a reserve of calcium. Each bone is a complex living organ that is made up of many cells, protein fibres and minerals. At birth, babies have about 300 bones. As they grow older, various bones fuse together and the typical adult human skeleton has 206 bones. Some individuals may have more or fewer bones because of anatomical variations. The breakdown is as follows: the axial skeleton has 80 bones composed of the skull with 28 bones and the torso with 52; the appendicular skeleton has 126 bones composed of the upper extremity with 64 (32 x 2) and the lower extremity with 62 (31 x 2). The axial skeleton runs along the body's midline axis and includes the skull, hyoid, auditory ossicles, ribs, sternum and the vertebral column. The appendicular skeleton includes the folowing regions: upper limbs, lower limbs, pelvic girdle and pectoral (shoulder) girdle. There are different types of bones, categorised by shape: flat, long, short and irregular. Flat bones are like those found in the skull, ribs, sternum and scapula. Long bones are the type found in the extremities, like the femur or thighbone in the leg or ulna in the arm. Short bones are found in the wrists and ankles and some of the irregular bones are found in the vertebrae and at the sutures in the skull. B The longest bone in our bodies is the femur (thigh bone). The smallest bone is the stirrup bone inside the ear. Bones are connected to other bones at joints. The different types of joints include: fixed joints such as in the skull, which consists of many bones; hinged joints such as in the fingers and toes; and ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulders and hips. Skeletal muscles , also known as striated muscles or striped muscles are muscles attached to bones and are responsible for skeletal movements. The centre of the bone is filled with marrow and this is surrounded by the hardened bone tissue itself. In bone, the extracellular matrix is composed of collagen with calcium phosphate deposited in it. Vitamin C is needed for collagen synthesis. Bone tissue is composed of repeating, circular units called Haversian systems . Within each Haversian system, there is a central canal where blood vessels and nerves can be found. This is surrounded by concentric layers of the matrix material called lamellae . In lamellae are spaces called lacunae which contain the osteocytes. Osteoblast is a large cell responsible for the synthesis and mineralisation of bone during both initial bone formation and later bone remodelling. Osteoblasts form a closely packed sheet on the surface of the bone, from which cellular processes extend through the developing bone. They produce many cell products, including the enzymes alkaline phosphatase and collagenase, growth factors, hormones such as osteocalcin and collagen (the structural protein of bones, tendons, ligaments and skin). A large part of the bone formed during the growth period is destroyed by specialised cells called osteoclasts in the growth process. A group of domesticated animals or plants having similar physical characteristics distinct from others of the same species. These characteristics have been produced by artificial selection. When bred together, animals of the same breed pass on these uniform traits to their offspring. For example, merino is a breed of sheep. The offspring produced as a result of breeding animals of one breed with other animals of another breed are known as crossbreeds or mixed breeds . Plant breeds are more commonly known as cultivars. Crosses between animal or plant variants above the level of breed/cultivar are referred to as hybrids. Breeding is the crossing and selection of animals and plants to change the characteristics of an existing breed (variety) or to produce a new animal, usually by artificial selection.

A nuclear reactor that produces more fissionable materials than it uses. The reactor is built with a core of fissionable plutonium, Pu^-239 and surrounded by a layer of U^-238. As the Pu^-239 undergoes spontaneous fission, it releases neutrons which convert U^-238 to Pu^-239. After all the U^-238 has been changed to Pu^-239, the reactor is refuelled. Some disadvantages of this breeder reactor are: (i) Pu^-239 is very toxic; (ii) the half-life of U^-239 is extremely long, about 24,000 years; this could create an almost impossible disposal problem if large amounts of this material are generated; (iii) because of the nature of the reactor core, water cannot be used as a coolant, so liquid sodium must be used. In the event of an accident a catastrophe could develop because sodium reacts violently with water and air.
